title: The Crocodile and the Wages
sum: In January 587 BC, with Jerusalem under siege and Egypt's army having just failed to save it, Ezekiel is told to turn on Pharaoh. He is a great sea monster lying in the Nile who says the river is his and that he made himself. The LORD will hook him, drag him onto dry land and leave him to the birds and animals. Egypt has been a reed staff for Israel: it snapped and cut the hand that leaned on it.

Then come two different promises about Egypt. It will be empty for forty years and then restored, but as a lowly kingdom (29:8-16). And, in the book's latest dated word, April 571 BC, Ezekiel says that Nebuchadnezzar got nothing from his long siege of Tyre, so the LORD gives him Egypt as his pay (29:17-21).
readings: Read as a prediction of events

Read this way, Egypt is struck by Babylon, emptied, scattered and then brought back as a small kingdom. Interpreters who read it so point to Nebuchadnezzar's attack on Egypt in 568/567 BC, Egypt's long loss of empire, and its rule by foreigners from Persia on. They say the forty years and the emptiness are not found in any record and must be read as a round figure or a poetic one.
Read as a mocking portrait of Pharaoh

Others stress that the chapter belongs to a family of oracles that mock a proud ruler (28:2; 31:2-18; Isaiah 14). The details of the crocodile, the hooks and the fish clinging to scales are about pride and a king's fall, not a program of future events.
Read as a prophecy that was revised

Verses 17 to 21 say plainly that an earlier word about Tyre (26:7-14) did not come out as the prophet had stated. The book keeps both words, the first and the correction. This can be taken as a sign that Ezekiel is honest about the gap, or, as critical readers take it, as a sign of how the book grew.

views.H: Hophra's army marched toward Jerusalem in 588/587 BC and withdrew (Jeremiah 37:5-11), so Judah's hope in Egypt had just failed when this word came. Egypt's later history is mixed: Nebuchadnezzar's clash with Amasis in 568/567 BC is recorded, but not a conquest, and no source shows Egypt empty for forty years. The siege of Tyre ended in about 573 BC, and no source describes a plundering, and 29:17-20 is the prophet's own comment on that.
views.C: Critical commentators ask why the forty years and the restoration (29:11-16) are placed between two oracles that do not mention them. Some commentators ask whether 29:12-16 is an addition that softens the verdict, since it repeats the language of Jeremiah 46:26 and Isaiah 19. The confession of 29:17-20 is the one dated word that is written after the event it comments on, and is commonly taken as evidence that Ezekiel or his school kept the earlier oracle and added the correction instead of rewriting it.
views.J: Rashi reads the forty years through the forty remaining years of famine decreed in Pharaoh's dream (Genesis 41). For the horn of 29:21 he says he has found no explanation and offers the rise of Persia under Cyrus, who freed the exiles (Isaiah 45:13). For the Tyre verse he says the booty was taken and then washed away by the sea. Other medieval commentators were not read for this part.
views.X: Christian readers have seen in the sea monster the older image of the dragon, an enemy of God overthrown (Isaiah 27:1; Revelation 12:9), though Ezekiel's text is about a king of Egypt. The promise of a lowly Egypt that is restored is often set beside Isaiah 19:19-25, where Egypt is blessed. The line that the LORD gave Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar for his work has been used in discussions of how God uses rulers who do not know him.
views.F: Readers who expect a future kingdom treat the forty years and Egypt's restoration as not yet fulfilled and place them beside Isaiah 19:19-25. Others hold the chapter was completed in the past. This site gives both as views; the text does not say when the forty years run.

deep.b: For chapters 29 to 32 the Plain English Translation is made from the Hebrew of the Leningrad Codex (AD 1008), verse by verse, starting from a word-for-word gloss. The Dead Sea Scrolls were checked through the Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcriptions (ETCBC dss): no Qumran or Masada copy preserves any verse of these four chapters, so the Leningrad Codex stands alone among the Hebrew witnesses here, with the written-and-read differences (Ketiv and Qere) listed by the site's text files. The Greek was read in Swete's edition, which prints Codex Vaticanus. The critical Greek of Ziegler and Papyrus 967 were not read for this part, and nothing in these chapters is said about what Papyrus 967 reads. The later Greek versions, the Targum and the Vulgate were not read either. Rashi was read in the Judaica Press translation on Sefaria for the verses where he is cited; Radak, Ibn Ezra and the Targum were not.

The four chapters carry six of the book's thirteen dates. In the order they sit in the book: 29:1 (tenth year, tenth month, twelfth day: about January 587 BC), 29:17 (twenty-seventh year, first month, first day: about April 571), 30:20 (eleventh year, first month, seventh day: spring 587), 31:1 (eleventh year, third month, first day: June 587), 32:1 (twelfth year, twelfth month, first day: about March 585) and 32:17 (twelfth year, fifteenth day, month not given: 585). The years are counted from Jehoiachin's exile in 597 BC and the calendar dates are the usual reckoning; some scholars date Jerusalem's fall to 587, which would move each by a year. The Egypt oracles are collected by subject, not by date. The Greek gives different dates in 29:1 and 32:1 (see the variants). Three of the six dates fall before the fall of Jerusalem (29:1, 30:20 and 31:1), two just after (32:1 and 32:17, once the news of the fall had come in 33:21), and one fifteen years later (29:17). In 32:17 the Hebrew gives no month; the Greek gives the first month.

Chapter 29 is prose. Chapter 30 is mostly prose, with a short poetic cry at 30:2-3. In chapter 31 the story of the tree (31:3-9) is the most poetic part, and 31:10-18 is its explanation in prose. In chapter 32 the lament of 32:2-8 is verse, 32:9-16 moves back toward prose, and 32:17-32, the descent to Sheol, is a chant with a repeated refrain in prose rhythm. Where the lines are drawn is a matter of judgment, and the Plain English Translation marks line breaks only where the verse is clearest.

Ezekiel mentions Egypt before these chapters: Israel's old idols from Egypt (20:7-8), the two sisters' lovers (23:3, 19-21), Zedekiah's treaty with Pharaoh (17:15-17). Here Egypt gets seven oracles: 29:1-16, 29:17-21, 30:1-19, 30:20-26, 31:1-18, 32:1-16 and 32:17-32. Babylon, the real conqueror, gets none. The nations in Jeremiah 46 (the same Pharaoh, the same Nebuchadnezzar, and the same cities Migdol, Memphis and Tahpanhes) and Isaiah 19 should be read beside these.

echoes: Jeremiah 43:8-13; Jeremiah 44:30; Jeremiah 46:13-26; Isaiah 19:1-25; Isaiah 36:6; Genesis 1:21; Isaiah 27:1; Exodus 7:5; Psalm 132:17; Ezekiel 26:7-14; Ezekiel 3:26-27; Ezekiel 24:27; Ezekiel 33:22

settings.to: Ezekiel's neighbors in the exile at Tel-abib, and the elders who sat before him; Pharaoh is addressed, but nothing says he heard it
settings.when: on the twelfth day of the tenth month of the tenth year, about January 587 BC, while Jerusalem was besieged and Egypt's relief army had come and gone
settings.why: to tell exiles who hoped Egypt would rescue Jerusalem, and who had urged Judah to trust it, that Egypt is a reed and will break; the people of Judah were told this twice already by Jeremiah (Jeremiah 37:5-10)
settings.readers: For the exiles who read the collected book after 586, the oracle explains why Egypt did not save the city, and the promise of a restored but lowly Egypt shows the LORD's care reaching a nation outside Israel.
views: Most commentators take the oracles against Egypt as spoken to the Judeans in Babylonia, to warn them off dependence on Egypt and give hope against Babylon's growing power. The nation addressed is not present.

settings.to: the exiles, twenty-two years after Ezekiel's first vision and fifteen years after the fall of Jerusalem
settings.when: on the first day of the first month of the twenty-seventh year, about April 571 BC, the latest date in the book
settings.why: to tell the exiles how to understand a prophecy about Tyre that had not come out as Ezekiel said: Nebuchadnezzar served the LORD at Tyre and is paid in Egypt; and to promise Israel strength and Ezekiel an open mouth
settings.readers: Later readers meet the oracle out of date order, placed with the others on Egypt; it asks them to read an earlier prophecy (26:7-14) in light of its aftermath.
views: The oracle is Ezekiel's own late word, written after the siege ended.

Critical commentators who trace how the book grew ask whether 29:21, and perhaps 29:17-20, were added after the earlier oracles; the dating in 29:17 puts the oracle itself in Ezekiel's own lifetime (571 BC), and every reading takes it as correcting the earlier word.

title: A Day for Egypt
sum: Egypt gets its own Day of the LORD. Ezekiel is told to wail: the day is near, a day of cloud. A sword will come on Egypt, and its allies will fall with it, Cush, Put, Lud and others. Fire and judgment move through the cities from the delta to Thebes. The agent is Nebuchadnezzar, "the most ruthless of the nations," who comes with the LORD's sword (30:10-12).

A second oracle, dated about April 587, says the LORD has already broken one of Pharaoh's arms, the army that failed at Jerusalem, and will break the other. The arms of the king of Babylon are made strong instead. The chapter ends where it began: the Egyptians scattered, and "Then they will know that I am the LORD."
readings: Read as the Day of the LORD
The cry "Alas for the day!" is the language of Joel, Obadiah and Isaiah 13. Egypt's fall is one case of the universal Day, when the LORD settles accounts with the nations and their gods.
Read as history seen in advance
The long list of cities is more like a map of a campaign than a poem, and it matches the Babylonian threat to Egypt in Jeremiah 46:13-26 and in the clash of 568/567 BC.

views.H: The two oracles bracket a failed Egyptian rescue. The arm already broken is the defeat that sent Hophra's army home (Jeremiah 37:5-11), and the cities listed are those where Judean refugees had gone (Jeremiah 43:7-9; 44:1). No source records the destruction of every place in this chapter. Thebes, Tanis and Memphis all continued to be great cities.
views.C: Commentators note that the cities list is in the shape of an oracle against the nations (Jeremiah 46:14; Nahum 3:8-10), and that 30:1-19 is a collection of short pieces joined by "thus says" openings (30:2, 6, 10, 13). The Greek text has several different names and readings, which shows that the list was handled freely in transmission.
views.J: Rashi takes "the people of the covenant land" (30:5) as lands bound to Egypt by treaty. The Day of the LORD is a main theme of the prophets in Jewish reading, and Ezekiel's chapter is the Egyptian part of it. Other medieval commentators were not read for this part.
views.X: Christian readers have joined the "day of the LORD" here to the day in Isaiah, Joel and Zephaniah, and to the New Testament use of the same phrase for the return of Christ (1 Thessalonians 5:2). The broken arm of Pharaoh has been used as a picture of a power that has been broken once and will be broken again.
views.F: Readers who look for a day still to come read 30:3 as part of the final Day of the LORD, in which Egypt shares. Readers who place the chapter in the past read it as fulfilled in the Babylonian campaigns.

deep.b: The list of 30:13-18 runs from Memphis in the north through the Delta and Upper Egypt: Memphis, Pathros, Zoan (Tanis), Thebes (No), Sin (Pelusium), On (Heliopolis), Pi-beseth (Bubastis) and Tahpanhes (Daphnae). The peoples of 30:5 are Egypt's soldiers and allies. Names such as Kub are known only here. See the notes for the Greek forms.

echoes: Joel 1:15; Obadiah 15; Isaiah 13:6; Isaiah 18:1-2; Jeremiah 46:9-26; Jeremiah 43:7-13; Leviticus 26:13; Nahum 3:8-10; Jeremiah 48:25

settings.what: The Day of the LORD against Egypt
settings.to: the Judean exiles in Babylonia, who feared Babylon and trusted Egypt; Egypt and its allies are named but not addressed
settings.when: undated in the Hebrew, between the oracle of 29:1 (January 587 BC) and 30:20 (spring 587)
settings.why: to show the exiles that Egypt's fall belongs to God's plan and so is no cause for panic or for hope in Egypt; and to bring the 'Day' that had fallen on Judah (7:5-12) to the nations that stood by
settings.readers: Later readers saw Egypt's fate as an instance of the Day of the LORD that comes on all nations.

settings.to: the exiles, a few months after Egypt's army failed at Jerusalem
settings.when: on the seventh day of the first month of the eleventh year, spring 587 BC, a year before Jerusalem fell
settings.why: to tell hearers who counted on Egypt that the defeat was only the first blow, and that the sword of Babylon was the LORD's
settings.readers: Later readers saw how Jerusalem's hope in Egypt was broken in advance of the city's fall.

title: The Cedar of Lebanon
sum: A year and a month before the city fell, Ezekiel asks Pharaoh a question: whom are you like in your greatness? The answer is a story about a tree. Assyria was a cedar in Lebanon, taller than every tree, fed by the deep, with birds in its branches and nations in its shade. Even the trees of the garden of God envied it.

Then it grew proud. The LORD gave it to a mighty ruler of the nations and foreigners cut it down. The earth mourned. In the end it went down to Sheol and the Pit with every other tree, and the trees of Eden were comforted. The last verse gives the point: this is Pharaoh and all his multitude.
readings: Read as a fable of Assyria
In the Hebrew text the tree is Assyria, an empire that fell in 612 to 609 BC while the exiles could still remember. The fable teaches Egypt by showing a greater power already gone.
Read as a fable of Pharaoh (a conjecture)

If the Hebrew is changed in 31:3 to read "a pine, a cedar" (a modern conjecture; no manuscript read for this part has it, and the Greek has Assyria), the tree is Egypt itself from the start. Either way the closing verse makes the tree Pharaoh.
Read as a garden-of-God story
The cedar is the greatest tree in Eden, and the setting has been compared with the tale of the first man in chapter 28. Eden here is a place in the story, not a history lesson.

views.H: Assyria's fall was recent history, and everybody in the exile knew it. Egypt had been Assyria's last ally (2 Kings 23:29). By setting Pharaoh beside the empire that died, Ezekiel puts Egypt's situation in the plainest terms: the greater tree fell.
views.C: The first verses are puzzling in the Hebrew: some editors conjecture that 31:3 names a tree (te'ashur) and not Assyria; the Hebrew and the Greek both have Assyria. 31:10 slips between "you" and "it." 31:14 has a hard word. Commentators treat 31:3-9 as an older poem or a poem composed for this occasion, with 31:10-18 as its explanation.
views.J: Rashi reads "Behold Assyria" as a reference to a power that has already fallen ("which I have already cast down"). Other medieval Jewish commentators were not read for this part.
views.X: Christian readers have pointed to the same tree in Daniel 4:10-12, 20-22, and the birds in the branches and the beasts in the shade return in Jesus' mustard seed parable (Matthew 13:31-32; compare Ezekiel 17:22-24). The proud tree cut down has often been read as a picture of pride.
views.F: No part of this chapter is usually read as still to come.

deep.b: The trees of Eden are named four times in the chapter (31:8, 9, 16, 18). Ezekiel 28:11-19 uses Eden for the king of Tyre, and 36:35 uses it for the land restored. In this chapter, Eden is a forest where trees envy each other, and the cedar is greater than all, yet goes down to the same place as the rest. See the note at 31:8 for the other Bible texts on the garden.

The tree goes down to Sheol, the world of the dead, here and in the next chapter. Most of the chapter's vocabulary (the deep, the Pit, the earth below, the uncircumcised) comes again in 32:17-32. The tree also takes others down with it: those who lived in its shade are the "arm" that falls with it (31:17), as Pharaoh's allies fall in chapter 30.

echoes: Judges 9:15; Isaiah 2:13; Isaiah 14:8; Ezekiel 17:22-24; Daniel 4:10-12; Genesis 2:8-9; Ezekiel 28:13; Ezekiel 36:35; Matthew 13:31-32

settings.to: Pharaoh and his multitude, as the text says (31:2); in practice the Judean exiles who heard or read it
settings.when: on the first day of the third month of the eleventh year, about June 587 BC, some thirteen months before Jerusalem fell
settings.why: to teach by comparison: the greatest empire the exiles remembered, Assyria, was gone, so Egypt's hope to outlast Babylon was empty
settings.readers: Later readers could read it as a parable of pride at any time, and it fits the pattern of Daniel 4.
views: The Hebrew text names Assyria and the tree is the earlier empire.
A modern conjecture changes 31:3 to 'a pine' (te'ashur), so that the tree is Egypt from the beginning and Assyria does not appear. No manuscript read for this part has it.

title: The Dirge and the Descent
sum: Ezekiel is told to sing a lament over Pharaoh, a young lion who is really a sea monster, churning the Nile with his feet. God will net him with many peoples and throw him on dry land, and the earth will drink his blood. The heavens go dark. Many nations will shudder, and the sword of Babylon will fall on Egypt's multitude. The Nile will settle and run like oil.

A second word, dated the fifteenth of a month the Hebrew does not name (two weeks later if it is the twelfth month; the Greek says the first month), sends Egypt down to the Pit. The scene is Sheol: the dead of Assyria, Elam, Meshech and Tubal, Edom, the leaders of the north and Sidon lie in their graves, each with a multitude, each killed by the sword and each "uncircumcised." Pharaoh will see them and be comforted.
readings: Read as a funeral satire

The chapter is a funeral lament for a man who is still alive, and its details are meant to mock. Egyptians were famous for the care they gave their dead kings; to give Pharaoh a grave among foreigners cut down by the sword was the worst insult.
Read as a picture of the world of the dead

Sheol appears here as a place, with graves, ranks, rooms and speech. Readers who take the chapter as a source for what the Old Testament believed about the dead use it beside Isaiah 14, Job 26 and Psalm 88; others hold that the picture is satire and not a doctrine.

views.H: The first lament comes about March 585 BC, a few months after the news of Jerusalem's fall reached Ezekiel (33:21). Babylon's sword is named (32:11). The second word lists peoples already dead (Assyria, Elam) and peoples whose end lay ahead (Edom, Sidon). The usual explanation is that Ezekiel speaks of them as already in the Pit because his oracles against them have been spoken.
views.C: The Greek differs here more than anywhere else in these chapters: it puts the words of 32:19 into its 32:21 (spoken by the giants), shortens 32:25, and names Assyria's rulers in place of Edom and the Sidonians. Commentators split on whether the Hebrew expanded a shorter text or the Greek translator abridged a long and repetitive one. The repetition in 32:22-30, with its fixed refrain, is part of the form of a chant.
views.J: Medieval Jewish commentators on this chapter were not read for this part. The picture of Sheol as a place with ranks of the dead belongs to the shared background of Isaiah 14 and the later rabbinic literature on the world to come.
views.X: Christian readers have set the chapter beside Jesus' picture of the dead (Luke 16:19-31) and the Greek Hades. Many treat it as a satire of pride, not as a map of the afterlife. The church has read the sea monster as an image of the devil in other texts; this chapter's monster is a human king.
views.F: The chapter is not usually read as describing the future; the descent to the Pit is read as a literary picture of defeat.

deep.b: The roll in 32:22-30 is Assyria, Elam, Meshech and Tubal, Edom, "the leaders of the north" and the Sidonians. They are each "killed by the sword" and "uncircumcised," and each has a multitude around its grave. Their common mark is the terror they spread in the land of the living. The last verse (32:32) says either that the LORD had put his own terror in that land (the Masoretic Qere, which the Plain English Translation follows) or that Pharaoh had spread his (the written Ketiv and the Greek); see the variant. This is the nations' roll, with Egypt's name at its head and foot (32:18-21, 31-32).

echoes: Isaiah 14:9-11; Isaiah 19:5-10; Exodus 10:21-23; Exodus 7:19-21; 2 Samuel 1:17-27; Ezekiel 19:1-14; Ezekiel 26:17-21; Ezekiel 28:10; Jeremiah 9:25-26; Job 26:5

settings.to: the exiles; the song is addressed to Pharaoh but is meant to be chanted by 'the daughters of the nations' (32:16)
settings.when: on the first day of the twelfth month of the twelfth year, about March 585 BC; the Greek says the tenth month
settings.why: to give the news of Jerusalem's fall a place in a larger story: the proud empires, including Egypt, end in the same ruin, and Babylon is the sword of the LORD
settings.readers: Later readers hear the song as a satire of any ruler who claims to be a god.

settings.to: the exiles; the fifteenth day falls two weeks after the preceding lament if the month is the twelfth, but the Hebrew does not give the month (the Greek says the first month)
settings.when: on the fifteenth day of the month, in the twelfth year, 585 BC
settings.why: to tell the exiles that Egypt's multitude joins the nations whose terror has ended in the Pit, and that Pharaoh will lie among them; the closing verse (32:32) sets the terror these nations spread beside the terror the LORD had put in the land of the living, or Pharaoh's own, depending on the reading
settings.readers: Later readers place the chapter at the end of the oracles against the nations as the last word on the world's empires.
